issues.item: Sleeping Alone: Sleeping alone or in an unfamiliar place
issues.explanation: The trigger set is hard to reconcile as a coherent pattern for a trauma-to-a-loved-one case: 'Cars hit by accident' suggests a specific road-traffic trauma cue, while 'Sleeping alone or in an unfamiliar place' implies separation/safety-context triggering. These could coexist, but without any supporting memory or appraisal content about separation, they look clinically mismatched within the trigger node.

issues.item: Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident
issues.explanation: 'I was betrayed by someone I trusted' is difficult to reconcile with the rest of the profile. The memory items describe vivid sensory re-experiencing of a frightening event, and the other appraisals emphasize unfairness and generalized vigilance, but nothing else suggests interpersonal betrayal. For a trauma-to-a-loved-one formulation, this appraisal would usually require supporting context (e.g. trusted person caused or enabled the harm), which is absent here.

The trigger profile is only weakly coherent with the stated trauma type of trauma to a loved one. 'Workplace' as a major trigger is hard to reconcile unless the loved-one trauma happened in the workplace or through occupational exposure, which is not reflected elsewhere in the profile. The other triggers (cars hit by accident, alcohol smell) imply a specific accident scene, making 'workplace' stand out as clinically questionable rather than part of the same trigger network.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted
issues.explanation: 'Betrayal by someone I trusted' points toward an interpersonal trauma formulation, but the rest of the profile centers on sensory accident-related reminders and vivid perceptual memory. For a trauma-to-a-loved-one presentation, this appraisal is difficult to integrate unless the loved one's trauma directly involved trusted-person betrayal, which is not supported by the other selected items.

issues.item: Constant Vigilance: I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next
issues.explanation: The Negative Appraisals node contains two items that are hard to reconcile with the trauma type and with each other. 'Constant Vigilance' implies an ongoing sense of current danger, but the formulation has no active Threat links and the rest of the profile is focused on accident-related reminders and vivid sensory memory rather than present threat. 'Self-Blame' is also difficult to fit with a loved-one accident trauma in this profile, because no other item suggests the patient had a causally responsible role in the event; combined with the injustice item, it creates a mixed appraisal pattern that lacks a clear coherent basis in the rest of the report.

issues.item: Injustice: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it
issues.explanation: Within the Negative Appraisals node, strong endorsement of both injustice/external blame ('nothing has been done about it') and self-blame for causing the event pulls in opposing directions and is difficult to reconcile as the same dominant appraisal without additional context. For a trauma to a loved one, these two appraisals can coexist in milder form, but selected together as core items they suggest conflicting attribution styles within the same node.

vignette:
Mere Tuilagi is a 71-year-old Fijian-American woman who has served as a police officer for over three decades, a career defined by her conviction that vigilance and discipline could hold the worst of the world at bay. She is married, the mother of adult children, and by most external measures a woman of considerable competence and composure. She presented for psychological assessment with a PCL-5 score of 65, describing a level of distress she had quietly endured for nearly two years before her husband finally persuaded her to seek help.

The event that precipitated her symptoms occurred on an evening when Mere had agreed to drive her younger sister, Leilani, to a family gathering across town. Mere had noticed, when she picked Leilani up, that her sister smelled faintly of alcohol - a detail she registered and then set aside, telling herself it was nothing, that Leilani was fine, that they weren't far. She did not say anything. Partway through the journey, a driver who had run a red light struck the passenger side of Mere's vehicle with full force. Leilani sustained severe traumatic brain injuries. The sounds of impact - the shattering of glass, the deep metallic crumple of the door, Leilani's single sharp cry - were the last things Mere heard before the world went briefly silent. Leilani survived but required months of rehabilitation and retains lasting cognitive deficits. Mere walked away with minor injuries.

In the weeks that followed, Mere's memories of the collision settled into a form that offered no relief. They came as vivid, detailed images - the precise angle of the other car, the way the passenger window exploded inward, the particular quality of the afternoon light - accompanied by sounds she could not silence: the impact, the cry, the sudden absence of her sister's voice. She had come to believe, with a certainty that felt like knowledge rather than interpretation, that she had caused what happened to Leilani. She had seen the smell of alcohol and said nothing. She had chosen that route. She had not been watchful enough, and Leilani had paid for it.

This conviction - that she had failed to protect her sister when protection was entirely within her power - became the lens through which she understood not only the accident but herself. She was certain that her inaction that evening was the reason harm had come, and she had arrived at a broader and more frightening conclusion: that she was simply unable to prevent bad things from happening to the people she loved, no matter how hard she tried or how carefully she watched.

At work, the consequences of these beliefs became woven into her daily life in ways that were impossible to ignore. Mere's role regularly brings her to the scenes of traffic collisions - the crumpled hoods, the deployed airbags, the geometry of impact preserved in metal and glass. Each scene now lands with a weight it never carried before. The sight of a car struck from the side stops her mid-thought, pulling her back to the passenger door caving inward. She had begun arriving at collision scenes later than she once would have, finding reasons to let younger colleagues take the lead, telling herself she was mentoring them. When accident reports were discussed at briefings, she found reasons to step out. A colleague once opened a can of beer at a retirement party, and Mere left the room before she could account for why.

Outside work she had stopped driving with passengers altogether, telling her husband she preferred he take the wheel when they went out together. He had accepted this for months before he understood it was not a preference but a wall she had built and could no longer see past.

What finally brought Mere to seek help was not a single event but an accumulation: the growing distance from her husband, who told her gently that she had become unreachable; the awareness that her avoidance was now visible to her colleagues; and a quiet, devastating moment when her granddaughter asked why Nana never drove her anywhere anymore. She came to the intake session composed and precise in her language, as she had been trained to be. What she most feared, she said, was that the person she had been - someone who could protect the people she loved - was simply gone. What she most hoped was that she was wrong.
